slides.title: Markov Decision Processes, Policies, and Value Iteration
Sequence models connect observations across time or space
A Markov model starts with state, an initial distribution, and transitions
The Markov assumption shortens the chain-rule history
Given the present, earlier history adds no information about the next state
An unrolled first-order chain is a Bayesian network
One transition model has three equivalent representations
From all sun, one step produces 0.9 sun and 0.1 rain
Forward prediction repeatedly applies the same transition operator
A stationary distribution is a fixed point—not a universal convergence promise
A Markov chain predicts; an MDP adds choices and consequences
An MDP is the tuple ⟨S, A, P, R, γ⟩
Actions change transition distributions; they do not guarantee outcomes
Reward is the formal objective—not a label for what humans value
Return adds immediate and discounted future rewards
A policy chooses; a value function predicts long-run return
Bellman expectation decomposes value into one step plus the remainder
Policy evaluation averages; optimal control maximizes
A Bellman optimality backup compares every action at one state
Value iteration applies Bellman optimality synchronously until change is small
Watch value information move through a 3×3 gridworld
A small Bellman residual is solver evidence, not real-world validation
Once values stabilize, one-step lookahead yields a greedy policy
An elegant solution can still optimize the wrong model
Model the future, choose a policy, and defend the assumptions
